subject: DBMS
_note: Content keyed by concept code. Only 3NF carries the full TeachBack rubric (learning + expected_concepts + misconceptions + knowledge_chunks). Sibling concepts carry a summary so the curriculum reads coherently; their TeachBack loop is disabled in the MVP.

FD.summary: A functional dependency X → Y means the value of X uniquely determines the value of Y. Functional dependencies are the language in which all normal forms are defined.

learning.key_idea: X → Y holds when two rows that agree on X must also agree on Y.

1NF.summary: A relation is in First Normal Form when every attribute holds a single, atomic value — no repeating groups or multi-valued cells.

learning.key_idea: 1NF removes multi-valued and composite attributes: one cell, one value.

2NF.summary: A relation is in Second Normal Form when it is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key — no partial dependencies on part of a composite key.

learning.key_idea: 2NF removes partial dependencies: non-key attributes must depend on the entire key, not just part of it.

3NF.summary: A relation is in Third Normal Form when it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key — every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

learning.key_idea: A relation is in 3NF if it is already in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies: no non-key attribute may be determined by another non-key attribute. Informally — every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
learning.explanation:
Third Normal Form builds directly on Second Normal Form. 2NF removes partial dependencies (a non-key attribute depending on only part of a composite key). 3NF removes the next problem: transitive dependencies.

A transitive dependency exists when a non-key attribute depends on the key only indirectly, through another non-key attribute. If A is the key and A → B and B → C, then C depends on A transitively (A → B → C). Even though the relation may already be in 2NF, that indirect chain still causes update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.

The formal statement uses prime and non-prime attributes: a relation is in 3NF if, for every functional dependency X → A, at least one of the following holds — X is a superkey, or A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key). This is stricter than 2NF but slightly looser than BCNF.
learning.example: Consider STUDENT(StudentID, Dept, DeptHead) with StudentID → Dept and Dept → DeptHead. StudentID is the key, so DeptHead depends on it only transitively: StudentID → Dept → DeptHead. This violates 3NF. Decompose into STUDENT(StudentID, Dept) and DEPARTMENT(Dept, DeptHead). Now every non-key attribute depends directly on its table's key, and no information is lost (the join on Dept reconstructs the original).
learning.common_mistake: Assuming that once partial dependencies are removed (i.e. the relation reaches 2NF), it is automatically in 3NF. 2NF only handles partial dependencies; 3NF additionally eliminates transitive dependencies. A relation can be firmly in 2NF and still violate 3NF.
learning.teachback_prompt: Explain Third Normal Form (3NF) in your own words — what it requires, and how it differs from 2NF. Imagine you're teaching a classmate who already understands 2NF.

followups.transitive_dependency: Consider R(StudentID, Dept, DeptHead) with StudentID → Dept and Dept → DeptHead. Explain precisely which dependency violates 3NF, and show how you would decompose R to remove it.
followups.non_prime_attribute: In a relation with candidate key {A}, which attributes are 'prime' and which are 'non-prime'? Use the formal 3NF rule — for every FD X → Y, X is a superkey or Y is prime — to explain why that distinction matters.

learning.default_followup: Give your own example of a relation that is in 2NF but not in 3NF, and show the decomposition that brings it to 3NF.

expected_concepts.label: Functional dependency
expected_concepts.description: 3NF is defined in terms of functional dependencies — which attributes determine which others.

expected_concepts.label: Candidate key
expected_concepts.description: 3NF is always judged relative to the candidate key(s) of the relation.

expected_concepts.label: 2NF foundation
expected_concepts.description: A relation must already be in 2NF — no non-key attribute may partially depend on a composite key.

expected_concepts.label: Dependency on the key
expected_concepts.description: Every non-key attribute must be determined by the key itself, not by another non-key attribute.

expected_concepts.label: Transitive dependency
expected_concepts.description: 3NF forbids transitive dependencies: a non-key attribute must not depend on the key indirectly through another non-key attribute (A → B → C).

expected_concepts.label: Prime attribute
expected_concepts.description: The precise definition of 3NF is stated with prime and non-prime attributes: for every functional dependency X → A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key). Naming which attributes are prime versus non-prime makes your 3NF check rigorous rather than intuitive.

expected_concepts.label: Worked example
expected_concepts.description: A strong answer grounds 3NF in a concrete relation and its functional dependencies.

misconceptions.title: Confusing 2NF with 3NF
misconceptions.description: Your explanation stops at removing partial dependencies, which is exactly what 2NF guarantees — it treats reaching 2NF as sufficient for 3NF.
misconceptions.why_it_matters: 3NF goes further: it also forbids transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute is determined by another non-key attribute rather than directly by the key. A relation can satisfy 2NF and still violate 3NF, so the transitive-dependency check is exactly what distinguishes the two.

knowledge_chunks.title: Definition of 3NF
knowledge_chunks.text: A relation schema R is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A that holds on R, either X is a superkey of R, or A is a prime attribute (a member of some candidate key). Equivalently, R is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key.
knowledge_chunks.source: Elmasri & Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

knowledge_chunks.title: Transitive dependency
knowledge_chunks.text: A transitive dependency is a functional dependency in which a non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute rather than directly on a candidate key. If A → B and B → C hold, and B is not a candidate key, then C is transitively dependent on A. 3NF eliminates such transitive dependencies to remove update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.
knowledge_chunks.source: Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan, Database System Concepts

knowledge_chunks.title: 2NF versus 3NF
knowledge_chunks.text: Second Normal Form removes partial dependencies: every non-prime attribute must be fully functionally dependent on every candidate key. Third Normal Form is strictly stronger — in addition to satisfying 2NF, it removes transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on candidate keys. A relation can be in 2NF yet violate 3NF when a non-key attribute determines another non-key attribute.
knowledge_chunks.source: SPPU DBMS Unit III — Relational Database Design (course notes)

knowledge_chunks.title: Prime and non-prime attributes
knowledge_chunks.text: An attribute is called a prime attribute if it is a member of at least one candidate key; otherwise it is a non-prime attribute. Normal-form definitions from 2NF onward are stated in terms of how non-prime attributes depend on candidate keys, which is why identifying the candidate keys is the first step of any normalization analysis.
knowledge_chunks.source: Elmasri & Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

knowledge_chunks.title: Decomposition to 3NF
knowledge_chunks.text: When a relation violates 3NF because of a transitive dependency A → B → C, it is decomposed by projecting out the offending dependency: replace R(A, B, C) with R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). This lossless-join, dependency-preserving decomposition removes the anomaly while allowing the original relation to be reconstructed by a natural join on B.
knowledge_chunks.source: Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan, Database System Concepts

BCNF.summary: A relation is in Boyce–Codd Normal Form when, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X is a superkey. BCNF is stricter than 3NF and handles anomalies 3NF can leave behind.

learning.key_idea: BCNF requires the left side of every non-trivial functional dependency to be a superkey.

DECOMP.summary: Decomposition splits a relation into smaller relations to eliminate anomalies. A good decomposition is lossless-join (the original can be reconstructed) and, ideally, dependency-preserving.

learning.key_idea: Decomposition must be lossless-join so no information is created or destroyed when tables are split.
